messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 32
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Tutor
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 59

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Expressions of Anger: Other people expressing anger, even calmly, Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise, Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others, Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Liam Weber was a 32-year-old tutor who came to treatment exhausted, ashamed of how much smaller his life had become, and frightened by how quickly ordinary moments could turn menacing. The stalking had begun almost a year earlier after he had ended several sessions with an adult student who had become increasingly intrusive. At first it was unsettling rather than terrifying: repeated messages from new numbers, long emails that mixed apology with accusation, sightings of the same motorcycle idling across from his apartment building. What made it feel unmistakably dangerous was the persistence. He began noticing the rider outside the tutoring center where he worked, then near the grocery store, then behind him when he took a different route home. One evening he looked over his shoulder and saw the bike slow when he slowed. By the time he reached his building, his hands were shaking so badly he dropped his keys. After that, the sound of a motorcycle engine no longer registered as traffic; it landed in his body as proof that he had been found again.

In the weeks that followed, Liam became preoccupied with the idea that people were never what they seemed. The stalking had convinced him that a person could present as needy, polite, even calm, while hiding something coercive underneath. He had come to mistrust others broadly, and he doubted his own judgment most of all. He replayed early interactions with the student and was certain he should have recognized the danger sooner, should have said something different, should have done the right thing before it escalated. That self-doubt sharpened the force of his triggers. If he heard even mild anger in someone’s voice—a parent objecting to a scheduling issue, a stranger snapping at a cashier—his mind moved immediately to hidden menace. The controlled tone frightened him almost more than shouting; to Liam, calm anger meant someone was masking intention. Likewise, the sensation of being followed no longer needed much evidence. A pedestrian behind him for half a block or a car slowing near the curb could be enough to activate the belief that appearances were deceptive and that he could not trust himself to judge danger accurately.

Those beliefs gradually shaped how he lived. Because he no longer trusted other people’s motives, and because he was not sure he would make good decisions if something happened again, he started keeping emotional distance from his wife. He told himself he was protecting her from his tension, but privately he also felt he deserved to suffer and should not be comforted. When she reached for him at night, he would go still or pretend to be tired. He also stopped letting himself relax in any real way. If he noticed his body softening while watching television or sitting beside her on the couch, he would tense again, as if dropping his guard invited danger. In his mind, closeness and relaxation meant vulnerability, and vulnerability was exactly how people got hurt without seeing it coming.

That way of coping left him increasingly keyed up. Nights became especially difficult. He had trouble falling asleep and, when he did sleep, woke at small sounds and lay listening for an engine outside. Because he spent so much energy braced against comfort and held himself apart from the one person who might have soothed him, his sense of danger rarely came down. False alarms became common. He would jerk around in public, heart pounding, convinced for a few seconds that someone had stepped too close behind him. The more frequently this happened, the more potent the triggers became. A motorcycle passing the tutoring center could undo an entire afternoon. If he heard raised irritation in the hallway before a lesson, he found himself scanning faces, trying to determine who was hiding something. He began avoiding unfamiliar places altogether because not knowing the exits, the parking layout, or who might be waiting there felt intolerable. His world narrowed to routes he had memorized and rooms where he could keep the door in view.

This had begun to affect his work. As a tutor, he often met students in libraries, homes, and learning centers, but now he pushed for online sessions or refused new locations outright. If a student’s parent expressed annoyance, even calmly, he struggled to stay focused on the material; part of him was already tracking tone, posture, and whether anyone else was in the building. On bad days he felt followed walking from his car to the center, and once inside he checked the windows for motorcycles before he could begin teaching. He knew these reactions sounded excessive when he described them, yet he was equally certain that people could not be trusted and that his own instincts had failed him before.

By the time he sought help, Liam was sleeping poorly, avoiding much of the city, and living with his wife more like a guarded roommate than a partner. What finally brought him in was an evening when she asked, not angrily but with obvious hurt, whether he was ever really with her anymore, and he felt the same jolt of alarm he felt with any trace of emotion in another person’s voice. He was frightened that this was becoming permanent—that he would keep mistaking ordinary life for danger, keep punishing himself, and keep withdrawing from the people he loved. More than anything, he wanted to be able to hear a motorcycle, or someone speaking sharply, or footsteps behind him, without feeling as though the stalking were happening all over again.
